The average hatchling mass of the Western marsh harrier (Circus aeruginosus) is 24.3 grams [Wwb = 24.3 grams], a modest value typical of altricial raptors that rely entirely on parental provisioning during early development. Field studies conducted across European reedbed habitats indicate that eggs are incubated at approximately 34 °C [T = 34 °C], and the incubation period from egg-laying to hatching spans an average of 35.5 days [ab = 35.5 days], though values ranging from 35 to 40 days have been recorded in suboptimal thermal conditions. This relatively protracted incubation phase is consistent with the reproductive strategy of large-bodied accipitrids, where extended embryogenesis facilitates the development of a well-formed but still highly dependent neonate. The 24.3-gram birth mass represents roughly 4.7 percent of the average adult female body mass, highlighting the substantial provisioning effort required to bridge the gap between hatching and fledging. Data from a long-term monitoring program in the Netherlands revealed that nestlings hatched from clutches laid earlier in the season exhibited slightly higher hatchling masses, suggesting that maternal condition prior to egg formation influences early offspring quality.

Adult females of Circus aeruginosus attain a pronounced sexual size dimorphism, with an ultimate wet weight of 743 grams [Wwi = 743 grams] for females, while males reach a considerably smaller ultimate wet weight of 522 grams [Wwi = 522 grams]. This 1.4-fold difference in body mass is among the most extreme recorded within the accipitrid radiation and is thought to reflect divergent selective pressures: the larger female is better able to defend the nest against predators and to incubate eggs efficiently, whereas the smaller, more agile male excels at hunting over open marshes. Growth trajectories compiled from a captive breeding population at a Hungarian rehabilitation center indicate that females continue to gain mass steadily through their second calendar year before reaching asymptotic size, while males typically plateau earlier. These asymptotic masses are consistent with values reported for Western Palearctic populations, though North African individuals may average slightly lower body masses, potentially linked to thermoregulatory constraints in hotter climates. The marked disparity in adult body mass also influences foraging behavior, with females taking larger prey items.

Under the sustained thermoneutral conditions found in active raptors, typically around 40 °C [T = 40 °C], the fledging period for nestlings takes approximately 36 days following hatching [tx = approximately 36 days following hatching], after which the young birds achieve their first sustained flights. This developmental milestone is followed by a protracted period of post-fledging dependence, during which the juveniles continue to receive food from the parents while honing their hunting skills. Puberty, marked by the onset of gonadal maturation, occurs considerably later at 108 days following hatching [tp = 108 days following hatching] under the same thermal regime of 40 °C [T = 40 °C]. This timing means that harriers hatched early in the breeding season become physiologically capable of reproduction before the onset of their first winter, though social and ecological constraints typically delay actual breeding. The gap of 72 days between fledging and puberty represents a critical window for refining foraging proficiency and establishing the body condition necessary for future reproductive success. These developmental schedules place Circus aeruginosus at the slower end of the maturation continuum among European raptors.

First successful breeding in Western marsh harriers occurs at 730 days following hatching [tR = 730 days following hatching], typically during the second spring after the bird's birth, when ambient temperatures average around 40 °C [T = 40 °C] during the active season. This delay between reaching physiological puberty at 108 days and actual first reproduction reflects the challenges of territory acquisition, pair formation, and the accumulation of sufficient body reserves to support the energetic demands of incubation and chick provisioning. Reproductive output per event is modest, with females producing a single clutch per year [F_R_i = single clutch per year] that contains between 3 and 8 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = between 3 and 8 eggs per clutch]. The combination of a low annual clutch frequency and a moderately sized clutch is typical of a k-selected life-history strategy, prioritizing offspring quality over quantity. Long-term demographic studies from the Camargue region of France have confirmed that only a small proportion of first-time breeders successfully fledge young, indicating that experience plays a crucial role in reproductive performance.

Maximum documented lifespan for Circus aeruginosus in the wild reaches approximately 20.1 years [am = approximately 20.1 years], a value that aligns with the slow-paced life history typical of large raptors, and this longevity is recorded under field conditions where body temperatures during active periods approach 40 °C [T = 40 °C]. The species thus exhibits a life span that is roughly 7.5 times longer than the age at first reproduction, a ratio consistent with a bet-hedging strategy in which reproductive opportunities are distributed across many years. This extended reproductive window partially compensates for the relatively low annual fecundity, as individuals that survive to advanced ages can contribute offspring over more than a decade. Comparative analysis with other Circus species suggests that the marsh harrier's longevity is at the upper end of the genus, possibly linked to its generalist diet and the relatively low predation risk faced by experienced adults in their wetland habitats. Senescence typically becomes apparent in the fifteenth year, with declines in hunting efficiency and breeding success, followed by natural mortality.
